summary: Sleeping-car magnate George Pullman built a company town outside Chicago, then cut wages without cutting rents in 1894, setting off a national railway boycott crushed by federal troops.

evidence.note: Pullman's birth in 1831 in upstate New York
Pullman renovates and then designs luxury sleeping cars, the Pioneer of 1864
Black porters hired at a fraction of conductor wages, called George by passengers
Land bought in 1880 and the company town built beside the factory
Town run like a fiefdom: no press, meetings or bars, inspections and evictions
Wages cut about 28 percent while rent and utilities kept high, workers fall into company debt
Long segment on Eugene Debs's background and founding of the American Railway Union
Union votes to exclude Black workers from the sympathy strike
Cleveland sends federal troops; injunction against union leaders; guardsmen fire on crowd
Pullman dies 1897; Illinois court strips him of the town in 1898

notes: Title names the strike but the host frames the story around George Pullman's life, so both are primary and the lifetime rule applies. inventor-engineer reflects his sleeping-car design work; medium confidence. A segment on an 1880s Atlantic article about the labor question was considered for propaganda-media but left out as context.
